subject: music
title: Taiwan campus folk: 'Sing our own songs' (1975–1985)
dek: In the mid-1970s Taiwanese university students mostly sang American and British pop. Within a few years they were writing and recording their own Mandarin songs, set to modern poems, campfire tunes and Indigenous melodies. This lesson follows the campus folk movement from Yang Hsien's 1975 concert and Li Shuang-tze's Coca-Cola protest through the song contests that turned it into an industry, the banned anthem Formosa, and Lo Ta-yu's 1982 album that ended the era and started modern Mandopop.
era: About 1975 to 1985, inside martial-law Taiwan, with roots in 1960s folk-song collecting and campus camp songs, and effects on Mandopop across Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore and mainland China
honesty: This lesson keeps to dates, names and events documented in the Chinese Wikipedia articles 校園民歌, 李雙澤, 楊弦, 金韻獎, 新格唱片, 美麗島 (歌曲), 胡德夫 and 龍的傳人, and the English Wikipedia articles on Lo Ta-yu, Hou Dejian, Chyi Yu, Descendants of the Dragon, Tomorrow Will Be Better, Teresa Teng, Xinyao, Nothing to My Name and Víctor Jara. Where those sources disagree, for example on whether Li Shuang-tze actually threw his Coke bottle, the lesson says so. The analysis sections are my own summary, not claims from a single source.

timeline.label: Folk-song collecting movement
timeline.detail: Composers Hsu Tsang-houei and Shih Wei-liang lead a field project recording traditional Han and Indigenous songs across Taiwan from 1965 to 1967, eventually collecting about 1,700 to 2,000 songs and discovering the folk singer Chen Da.

timeline.label: Taiwan leaves the United Nations
timeline.detail: The Republic of China loses its UN seat. Young people begin asking what their own culture is, while most still listen to Western pop.

timeline.label: Yang Hsien sets Yu Kwang-chung to music
timeline.detail: Graduate student Yang Hsien performs his setting of Yu Kwang-chung's poem 鄉愁四韻 at a concert by Hu Defu, with Yu in the audience.

timeline.label: Modern folk concert at Zhongshan Hall
timeline.detail: Yang Hsien's concert at Taipei Zhongshan Hall launches the album 中國現代民歌集. Its first pressing of 30,000 copies sells out within a month.

timeline.label: The Tamkang incident
timeline.detail: At a Western folk concert at Tamkang College, Li Shuang-tze walks on stage with a bottle of Coca-Cola, sings Taiwanese folk songs and asks why the audience paid to hear Chinese people sing foreign songs.

timeline.label: Our Songs, the Golden Melody contest and Li's death
timeline.detail: Radio host Tao Hsiao-ching records the album 我們的歌 with eight singers. Sony's Taiwan label Synco starts the 金韻獎 contest (final on 26 June). Li Shuang-tze drowns on 10 September while trying to save a swimmer.

timeline.label: Chyi Yu wins; Descendants of the Dragon
timeline.detail: Chyi Yu wins the second 金韻獎 singing Joan Baez's Diamonds & Rust. Haishan Records launches its rival contest 民謠風. After the United States announces recognition of Beijing on 15 December, Hou Dejian writes 龍的傳人.

timeline.label: The Olive Tree and the Formosa magazine
timeline.detail: Chyi Yu releases 橄欖樹, written by Li Tai-hsiang from a text by Sanmao. Opposition activists name their magazine 美麗島 after Li Shuang-tze's song; the Kaohsiung Incident follows in December.

timeline.label: Formosa is banned
timeline.detail: The Government Information Office formally lists 美麗島 as a banned song. Lee Chien-fu's recording of 龍的傳人 becomes a national hit.

timeline.label: Lo Ta-yu's Pedantry
timeline.detail: Rock Records releases Lo Ta-yu's 之乎者也, a sharp, rock-based album about modern Taiwanese life. Around the same time Haishan Records closes, and the song-contest boom is over.

timeline.label: Hou Dejian goes to the mainland
timeline.detail: Hou Dejian leaves Taiwan for the People's Republic of China in defiance of a travel ban, and his song is reinterpreted as a call for Chinese unity.

timeline.label: Tomorrow Will Be Better
timeline.detail: Lo Ta-yu's charity single 明天會更好, modelled on Band Aid and We Are the World, is recorded by more than 60 singers from Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia, and released on 25 October with proceeds donated to Taiwan's Consumers' Foundation.

fun_fact.title: The contest was won with a Joan Baez song
fun_fact.text: The movement's slogan was 'sing our own songs', yet Chyi Yu won the 1978 金韻獎 singing Joan Baez's English-language Diamonds & Rust, and the first winner, Chen Ming-shao, also won with an English song. Even the founding protest at Tamkang ended with Li Shuang-tze singing Bob Dylan's Blowin' in the Wind. The American folk revival was both the thing the students were reacting against and the model they borrowed from.

sections.title: Before campus folk: Western pop, camp songs and field recordings

blocks.text: In the early 1970s the music young Taiwanese people loved most was Western pop. University students sang American and British hits in coffee houses and at parties, while the Mandarin pop industry mostly produced film songs and ballads. Martial law had been in force since 1949, every record had to be approved by the Government Information Office, and songs could be banned for their lyrics.

Two quieter traditions were already feeding the movement that followed. In the mid-1960s the composers Hsu Tsang-houei and Shih Wei-liang led a folk-song collecting project, travelling around Taiwan from 1965 to 1967 to record traditional Han and Indigenous music. They gathered about 1,700 to 2,000 songs and found singers such as Chen Da, an elderly Hengchun folk singer who accompanied himself on the moon lute. At the same time, student clubs and the China Youth Corps summer camps spread simple singalong songs, some adapted from Indigenous melodies and given Mandarin words, through pocket songbooks.

Politics then gave students a reason to look inward. In 1971 the Republic of China lost its seat at the United Nations, and in 1972 Japan broke diplomatic relations and Richard Nixon visited Beijing. Many young people began asking why they sang other people's songs, and what their own songs would sound like.

sections.title: Yang Hsien and the modern poem as a song

blocks.text: Yang Hsien, a graduate student at National Taiwan University's institute of oceanography, liked to watch and sometimes join the performers at the Columbia coffee shop on Zhongshan North Road, where the Puyuma and Paiwan pianist Hu Defu played. In summer 1974, at one of Hu's concerts, Yang performed his own musical setting of 鄉愁四韻 (Four Rhymes of Nostalgia), a poem by Yu Kwang-chung, with Yu in the audience. Yu was pleased and encouraged him to set more poems from his collection 白玉苦瓜 (The White Jade Bitter Melon).

On 6 June 1975 Yang held a 'modern folk song creation concert' at Taipei Zhongshan Hall. The first half was English songs; the second half was his settings of Yu's poems, combining guitar, piano and violin with a feeling for classical Chinese imagery. The album that came out of it, 中國現代民歌集 (Collection of Modern Chinese Folk Songs), sold out its first pressing of 30,000 copies within a month. It is widely treated as the start of the modern folk movement, and Yang was later called its father.

The word 民歌, folk song, immediately caused an argument. Academic musicians said a folk song is created collectively, passed on orally and tested by time, so a graduate student's settings of a living poet could not be 'folk' at all. In 1978 Hsu Tsang-houei listed those criteria in print. The argument ran alongside the larger Nativist Literature Debate of 1977–1978, in which Yu Kwang-chung was on the opposite side from left-leaning writers.

sections.title: Li Shuang-tze and the Coca-Cola bottle

blocks.text: Li Shuang-tze, born in 1949 to an overseas Chinese family from the Philippines, came to Taiwan as a child, studied mathematics at Tamkang College and spent most of his time painting. Working around Taipei in 1972, he met Hu Defu at the Columbia coffee shop and asked him a famous question: 'You're Puyuma, right? Don't your people have your own songs? Sing one of your own.' Hu, who was performing to pay for his father's surgery, could not think of one at first, then remembered 美麗的稻穗 (Beautiful Rice Ears), a song his father used to sing.

On 3 December 1976 Tamkang held a Western folk concert hosted by the radio presenter Tao Hsiao-ching. Li walked on stage carrying a guitar and a bottle of Coca-Cola. He sang four Taiwanese songs, 補破網, 恆春之歌, 雨夜花 and 望春風, stopped partway through the patriotic 國父紀念歌 to ask why nobody was singing along, then sang Bob Dylan's Blowin' in the Wind and asked the audience why they had paid twenty dollars to hear Chinese people sing foreign songs. Students from a campus current-affairs club had been planted in the crowd to boo and to shout down the booing. The story that he smashed or threw the bottle is, according to Tao Hsiao-ching, a later myth; she says he never threw it.

The 'Tamkang incident' set off a debate in the campus weekly and gave the movement its slogan, 唱自己的歌, sing our own songs. Li wrote songs quickly after that, including 美麗島 (Formosa), adapted by the Tamkang professor Liang Jingfeng from Chen Hsiu-hsi's 1973 poem 台灣, and 少年中國 (Young China), based on a poem by Chiang Hsun. On 10 September 1977, before recording any of them, Li drowned at a beach in Tamsui while trying to save a foreign swimmer. He was 28.

Hu Defu and the Tamkang student Yang Tsu-chun spent the night before his funeral turning his manuscripts into performable songs, and 美麗島 was heard publicly for the first time at the funeral. Yang Tsu-chun recorded it on her 1979 album. The circle around Li, the teacher Wang Jin-ping and the left-wing magazine 夏潮 (China Tide) became known as the Tamkang–China Tide line, and it disliked what happened next: the commercial contests.

Electronics companies paid for much of the movement. Yang Hsien's album had been produced by a foundation named after Hung Chien-chuan, founder of Taiwan's National (Panasonic) electronics business, and as early as 1971 the appliance maker Kolin had backed a TV songwriting show to sell its brand. In 1977 Synco (新格), the record label of Sony's Taiwan joint venture, launched the 金韻獎 (Golden Melody) youth song contest. Its first final was held on 26 June 1977 and its winners included Chen Ming-shao and Bao Mei-sheng. The same year Tao Hsiao-ching recorded 我們的歌 (Our Songs) with eight singers including Hu Defu, Yang Hsien and Wu Chu-chu.

In 1978 Haishan Records, a local label that had grown rich on Huangmei opera film songs, started its own contest, 民謠風. Fans spoke of a Synco faction and a Haishan faction. Joseph Yeh (葉佳修), a Haishan figure, described Synco as polished and glamorous, with attractive singers and careful packaging, and Haishan as more natural and down to earth. Synco hired young classically trained musicians such as Chen Yang and Ma Shui-long behind the scenes, and the Amis composer Li Tai-hsiang recorded orchestral folk albums for the label.

The contests produced a generation of stars. Chyi Yu won in 1978 and Wang Hai-ling in 1979, and a young Jonathan Lee (李宗盛) took the top score in the 1979 group category with his own song. Tsai Chin came out of the Haishan side. Campus folk songs were usually gentle Mandarin ballads with acoustic guitar about mountains, rivers, youth and an imagined China, and many set the words of poets such as Yu Kwang-chung, Hsi Mu-jen, Sanmao and Chiang Hsun. A few were in Taiwanese Hokkien, such as Chien Shang-jen's 正月調.

The best-known song of the commercial years is 橄欖樹 (The Olive Tree), released by Chyi Yu in 1979. Li Tai-hsiang wrote the music to a text by the travel writer Sanmao, which began as a poem about a small donkey she met on a plain in Spain. Yang Tsu-chun translated it into Chinese, and Li Tai-hsiang, with Sanmao's agreement, changed the image from the donkey to an olive tree, and the song became a lasting anthem of wandering and longing.

sections.title: Two anthems pulled in opposite directions

blocks.text: Two campus songs show how politics took over the music. When the United States announced on 15 December 1978 that it would recognise the People's Republic of China, the student songwriter Hou Dejian, who had grown up in a military dependents' village in Kaohsiung, wrote 龍的傳人 (Descendants of the Dragon). Its lyrics describe the Yangtze and the Yellow River and call on the 'great dragon' to open its eyes. Lee Chien-fu's recording, released in 1980, topped the Minsheng Daily chart for fifteen weeks, and the government welcomed it as a patriotic song.

Then Hou left for the mainland in 1983 against a travel ban, and the song was banned in Taiwan for a few years while Beijing embraced it as a call for Chinese unity. Hou objected that people had misread him. In 1989 he joined the Tiananmen protests, changed 'appeasers' in the lyrics to 'dictators', and on 2 June began a hunger strike in the square with Liu Xiaobo, Zhou Duo and Gao Xin. On the morning of 4 June he helped negotiate the students' withdrawal from the square, and he was later expelled from China.

Li Shuang-tze's 美麗島 travelled the opposite way. In 1979 opposition (dangwai) activists named their magazine 美麗島 after it, and the Kaohsiung Incident of December 1979 is still called the Formosa Incident. The Government Information Office formally banned the song in 1980 because officials suspected it of Taiwanese independence sentiment. It survived anyway: Fan Yun led the students in singing it during the 1990 Wild Lily student movement, and Hu Defu sang it at Chen Shui-bian's inauguration celebration in 2000.

items: 龍的傳人 begins as a Taiwanese protest against Washington, becomes an anthem in Beijing, and ends up sung by protesters against Beijing.
美麗島 begins as a student's love song for the island's landscape and people, and becomes the soundtrack of the democracy movement.
Both show that under martial law, choosing whose songs to sing was itself a political act.

blocks.text: Lo Ta-yu, born in Taipei in 1954, finished medical school in Taichung to satisfy his family and then gave up medicine for music. He wrote film music and songs for others in the late 1970s, including 童年 (Childhood) for Sylvia Chang, and in 1982 Rock Records, a label founded only in 1980, released his first album, 之乎者也 (Pedantry). The title is made only of grammatical particles from classical Chinese, a joke at the expense of empty learning.

Pedantry mixed rock, folk and reggae with lyrics about urban emptiness, Confucian stiffness and a small town losing itself in 鹿港小鎮 (Lukang, the Little Town). Lo appeared in dark sunglasses, far from the clean-cut image of the contest singers. The album is often called the start of a new era of Mandarin pop, and his 1983 album 未來的主人翁 (Master of the Future) went further with 亞細亞的孤兒 (Orphan of Asia), named after Wu Zhuoliu's novel about Japanese colonial Taiwan.

In 1985 Lo wrote 明天會更好 (Tomorrow Will Be Better), modelled on Band Aid and We Are the World, which had raised money for Ethiopian famine relief. More than 60 singers from Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia recorded it, and it was released on 25 October 1985 with proceeds donated to Taiwan's Consumers' Foundation (消基會). Lo's first lyrics were so critical of society that singers walked out, and under martial law he was persuaded to let other songwriters rewrite them. He moved to New York and then to Hong Kong in 1986, citing political pressure on his work.

sections.title: What campus folk was really about

blocks.text: Campus folk was a search for identity carried out by students who were not allowed to discuss identity openly. Its slogan asked what 'our own' songs were, and different people gave different answers: the classical Chinese imagery of Yu Kwang-chung and Yang Hsien, the Taiwanese and Indigenous songs that Li Shuang-tze and Hu Defu wanted to recover, or simply songs about everyday student life. The vague, beautiful 'China' of many hits was safe under martial law; songs about Taiwan itself, like 美麗島, were not.

It was also an early lesson in how sponsors shape culture. Appliance makers and record labels turned a protest slogan into contests, compilations and TV specials within about two years. That commercial push gave Taiwan a professional songwriting industry, a generation of producers such as Jonathan Lee, and the model of the singer-songwriter that later Mandopop took for granted. It also smoothed the music into something polite, which is why the Tamkang circle rejected it and why Lo Ta-yu's harder sound felt like a break.

Finally, it is notable how many women carried the movement. Tao Hsiao-ching opened her radio show to young writers and organised Our Songs; Yang Tsu-chun preserved Li's songs and sang them at political events; Chyi Yu, Bao Mei-sheng, Chen Ming-shao and Tsai Chin were among its best-known voices; and Sanmao and Hsi Mu-jen supplied lyrics. At the Formosa magazine's launch party in 1979, the opposition activist Tien Meng-shu told Yang Tsu-chun in Hokkien to stop singing that 'pig song' in Mandarin; Yang later called this Hokkien chauvinism. It is a reminder that the movement's arguments were about language and ethnic identity as well as nation.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: In Britain and the United States, 1976–1977 was the year of punk, another youth movement built on the idea that ordinary people could make their own music without permission from the industry (see the punk lesson). The sound could not have been more different, but the impulse was related. Campus folk's direct model was the American folk revival of the early 1960s, the music of Joan Baez and Bob Dylan, which Taiwanese students knew from records (see the folk revival lesson).

In Chile, the Nueva Canción movement had already shown how dangerous folk songs could be. The singer Víctor Jara was killed on 16 September 1973, days after the military coup. In Taiwan nobody was killed for a campus song, but the banning of 美麗島 shows the same instinct in a softer authoritarian state.

Across the Chinese-speaking world, Taiwanese songs spread fast. Teresa Teng's ballads were smuggled into mainland China on cassette from about 1978, and The Olive Tree and other campus songs followed. Singapore developed its own student songwriting style, xinyao, in the late 1970s and 1980s, and Hong Kong developed 'city folk'. In Beijing, Cui Jian's Nothing to My Name started Chinese rock in the mid-1980s, and in 1989 Tiananmen protesters sang it alongside Hou Dejian's Descendants of the Dragon.

By the early 1980s the movement had faded. The 金韻獎 had held its last yearly contest in 1980, with one final edition in 1984, Haishan Records closed, and many singers went abroad to study, did military service or moved to Hong Kong and the mainland. Taiwan TV's 大學城 contest kept student songwriting alive from 1984 to 1993 and launched Sky Chang (張清芳). Rock Records, and UFO Records, founded by Rock Records people, built the Mandopop industry of the late 1980s and 1990s on the foundations campus folk had laid, and Synco itself was bought by Rock Records in 1993.

Some of the movement's people went in political directions. Hu Defu joined the dangwai movement and in December 1984 became the founding chair of the Alliance of Taiwan Aborigines, after seeing that many of the victims of that year's Haishan coal mine explosion were Indigenous. He recorded his first solo album only in 2005 and won Golden Melody Awards for songwriting and song of the year in 2006. In 2015 the 民歌40 concerts celebrated forty years since Yang Hsien's first show, and the campus songs remain fixtures of KTV and nostalgia for Taiwanese people born in the 1960s and early 1970s.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Campus folk asked 'what are our own songs?', and Taipei, Beijing, democracy activists and record companies all gave different answers. If cool dairy tells stories about Taiwanese women and culture, whose version of 'our own' will it tell, and who might feel left out of it?
